title: Agentic Support vs AI Chatbots: What's the Difference? | Pylon
summary: Chatbots answer questions. Agentic support fixes the issue, using account context and your tools. Here's the difference and why it matters for B2B.
body_markdown:
> **Agentic support, in one line:** AI agents that work a customer issue from start to finish. They look up the account, check your other tools, file bugs, update records, and pull in a person when a call needs judgment. A chatbot finds an answer and replies. That's where its job ends.


Most support teams have tried a chatbot by now.


It usually goes the same way. The bot handles the easy questions just fine. Then anything harder gets handed to a person, often with zero context attached, and your team starts from scratch.


Agentic support is the newer idea. It isn't just a smarter chatbot. It changes what the AI is actually on the hook for.


Here's the difference in simple terms, why it matters more for B2B teams, and what to look for when a vendor says they do it.


## What a chatbot actually does


A chatbot answers questions. Most modern ones run on a large language model and pull answers from your help center.


The flow is simple:


1. A customer asks a question in a chat widget.
2. The bot searches your docs.
3. It writes a reply.
4. If it can't answer, it hands off to a person.


That's genuinely useful. A good chatbot can take a real chunk of repetitive "how do I…" questions off your team's plate.


But it stops at the reply. It usually doesn't know who the customer is, what plan they're on, what they said in Slack last week, or whether there's an open bug that explains the problem. And it can't *do* anything in your other tools.


Chatbots are usually measured on **deflection** : how many conversations never reach a person.


## What agentic support does differently


Instead of a script ("answer this question"), the agent gets a goal ("resolve this issue"). To get there, it can:


- **Think it through.** Figure out what's going on before it replies.
- **Look at the account.** Plan, ARR, health, past conversations, call notes, open issues.
- **Use your tools.** Read from and write to your CRM, issue tracker, codebase, and data warehouse.
- **Get things done.** Update a field, file a bug, route to the right team, draft a reply, give a CSM a heads up.
- **Know when to stop.** Bring in a person when something needs approval or a judgment call.


Your team's job changes too. Instead of doing every lookup by hand, people review, approve, and make the calls that need a human. People and agents work the same queue together.


Agentic support is measured on **resolution** : did the issue actually get fixed, correctly, for the right customer?


## Side by side


**AI chatbot** **Agentic support**


**What it's trying to do** Answer the question and close the chat Fix the actual problem


**What it knows** Your help center Your help center, plus the account, past conversations, calls, open bugs, and code


**What it can do** Reply with text Reply, and also update records, file bugs, route tickets, and ping people


**Where it shows up** Usually a chat widget on your site Wherever customers already are: Slack, Microsoft Teams, email, chat, portals, and more


**Handing off to a person** "Let me get someone," often with no context A summary of what it checked and what it thinks should happen next


**Who it helps** Mostly the customer The customer and your own team (support, CS, product, engineering)


**How it's measured** Deflection rate Resolution rate, time to resolution, accuracy


## Why this matters more in B2B


In B2C, a lot of questions look the same, and each customer is one of many. A bot that answers "how do I reset my password?" thousands of times a day is doing real work.


B2B is different.


- **Every account is different.** The right answer depends on the customer's plan, setup, integrations, and contract. A $200K account and a free trial might need very different handling for the same question.
- **Customers talk in shared channels.** They reach you in Slack Connect or Microsoft Teams, not a chat bubble on your site. And there might be five people from the same company in the thread.
- **One issue touches several teams.** A "support question" is often a bug for engineering, a renewal risk for CS, and a feature request for product, all at once.
- **Mistakes cost more.** A wrong answer to a key account can show up at renewal time.


So B2B teams need AI that can see the account and act across tools, not just search docs.


A lot of teams also support B2B and B2C customers side by side. Sardine and Wispr Flow both run on Pylon for exactly that, so the same platform handles high-volume questions and the complex, account-specific ones.


## Here's what it looks like in practice


Say a customer posts in your shared Slack Connect channel: "Exports have been failing for us since this morning."


With a chatbot, that's the end of the road. You get "Sorry to hear that, let me connect you with someone," and a person starts digging.


With an agent, a lot happens before anyone on your team opens the thread:


1. **It checks the account.** Enterprise customer, annual contract, renewal coming up, health score dipped recently.
2. **It looks for a pattern.** Two other accounts reported the same export error today. Nothing in the issue tracker yet.
3. **It files the bug.** A Linear issue with the error details, the affected accounts, and links to each conversation.
4. **It updates the customer.** "We've confirmed the issue, engineering has it, and we'll update you here." If your team wants to review replies first, a person approves it before it goes out.
5. **It gives the CSM a heads up.** The account is up for renewal, so the CSM gets a short summary.
6. **It closes the loop.** When the Linear issue is fixed, the customer hears about it in the same thread.


Your team still owns the outcome. They just aren't spending 30 minutes on lookups to get there.


## You don't have to go fully autonomous on day one


Most teams ease in. It usually looks something like this:


1. **Assist.** The agent investigates and drafts. A person reviews and sends.
2. **Act with approval.** The agent suggests an action (file a bug, update a field, issue a credit) and a person says yes or no.
3. **Handle the common stuff.** The agent answers and closes well-understood questions on its own and brings in a person for everything else.
4. **Run workflows on autopilot.** Repeatable work like triage, tagging, routing, and knowledge-gap reports runs on a trigger or a schedule.


A good platform lets you pick the level per workflow and per action, and lets you test a change before it goes live.


## Questions to ask in a demo


If a vendor says they do agentic support, here's what's worth asking:


- **Context:** Does the agent know the account (plan, ARR, health, history) before it starts, or only what's in the help center?
- **Channels:** Does it work in Slack Connect, Microsoft Teams, email, and your portal, or just a website widget?
- **Actions:** What can it actually do in your CRM, issue tracker, and other tools? Can you limit permissions and require approval?
- **Handoff:** When a person takes over, what do they get? A blank ticket or a full summary?
- **Testing:** Can you try a change against past tickets before turning it on?
- **Setup:** Can your support ops team set it up in natural language, or does every workflow need an engineer?
- **Pricing:** Per resolution, per conversation, per seat, or usage credits? What happens to cost as volume grows?
- **Security:** SOC 2 Type II, data residency, audit logs, and controls on what agents can see.

## FAQ


### What is agentic support?


It's support where AI agents work an issue end to end. They think through the problem, use account context and your connected tools, and take action to resolve it. A person steps in for approvals and judgment calls.


### What's the difference between an AI agent and a chatbot?


A chatbot answers questions, usually from your help center, inside one conversation. An agent works toward a goal. It can look up account data, use your other tools, file a bug or update a record, and hand off with full context.


### Is agentic support just a better chatbot?


No. A chatbot's job ends at the reply. Agentic support is on the hook for the outcome, including the investigation and follow-up work around the reply.


### Do AI agents replace support teams?


No. Agents take on the lookups, triage, and repeat questions. People focus on judgment calls, complex accounts, and relationships. Most teams start with agents assisting people and expand from there.


### Why does agentic support matter for B2B companies?


B2B issues depend on the specific account, often show up in shared Slack or Teams channels, and usually involve several teams. An agent needs account context and the ability to act across tools to actually resolve them.


### Can agentic support work for B2C too?


Yes. Lots of companies support both. Pylon is purpose-built for B2B, and teams like Sardine and Wispr Flow use it for both their B2B and B2C customers.


### How is agentic support priced?


It depends on the vendor. Some charge per resolution or per conversation. Pylon charges for seats plus agentic credits, not per ticket, and its pricing is public on[usepylon.com/pricing](https://www.usepylon.com/pricing) : Professional is $89 per seat/month and Advanced is $139 per seat/month, both on an annual contract. Committed credit packages start at 5,000 credits, and pay-as-you-go is available when it's turned on for your account.


### Is Pylon an AI add-on for Zendesk or Intercom?


No. Pylon is a full help desk with AI agents built in, so teams switch to it from tools like Zendesk or Intercom rather than adding it on top. The agents and your team work from the same tickets and the same account context in one platform.
